extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, corporate/agency publicists, and PR students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for writing and formatting traditional and online news (press) releases aimed at media and key stakeholders, covering structure, style, distribution and etiquette. Includes both print/page and email/electronic release practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masthead / Name and Address of Source
rubrics_metrics.description: Masthead and/or Name and Address of News Release Source (example: WritingRX.com).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the organization/source name and address prominently at the top of the release (as a traditional masthead).

rubrics_metrics.name: Release Date / Release Status
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE' for most releases or indicate embargo with 'FOR RELEASE ON OR AFTER [date]'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embargo lengthy reports so recipients have time to digest and prepare stories; mark release date/status clearly at top.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact Information / Identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Include contact information: NAME OF CONTACT, Tel, E-mail; name, address, phone numbers (during and after hours) and e-mail of author and other contacts at the top of the first page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide 24/7 contact information when appropriate (e.g., hospitals, emergency services). Ensure media can reach someone quickly; include office and home phone/fax/email if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline (one-line, concise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Headline [one line, two lines maximum]: give recipients a snapshot of what the release covers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a pithy one-line headline that doesn't repeat the lead sentence. For email releases the subject line acts as the headline (many PR practitioners also put a headline in the email body).

rubrics_metrics.name: Link to Images / Multimedia (prefer hyperlinks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Link to images if available and needed; electronic releases can contain photos, audio and video but media prefer hyperlinks to these items rather than attachments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide links to a server where journalists can select/download assets; avoid attachments (attachments can contain viruses and complicate work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline
rubrics_metrics.description: Dateline [city, state, date of release] followed by text: the date of the release and place of origin should lead the first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start the first paragraph with the dateline (place and date) to lead into the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic Writing Style (AP standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meet the standards of journalistic writing — simple and direct language (factual, to the point, not 'pluggy'), short words, short sentences, short paragraphs, active verbs, meaningful quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow AP style, be accurate, credible, appropriately substantiated, properly punctuated and carefully proofread. Clear writing and newsworthy content are crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and Focus (use the 5 W's)
rubrics_metrics.description: As short as possible. One page is ideal, two OK, but three or more is too long unless the release constitutes a 'feature'. Give the media only what they need — usually the classic 5 W's (who, what, where, when and why).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fact sheets or attachments for supplemental material. Keep releases concise so editors can decide quickly whether to use the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typography and Print Formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Formatted for copying on one side of standard 8-1/2 x 11 plain white sheet; use same weight paper for each page and standard 10 pt. or 12 pt. 'serif' typeface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use serif (e.g., Times Roman) not sans serif; leave ample margins (at least 1 inch), indent paragraphs, use unjustified right margins, number pages, put 'more' or 'continued' at the bottom of each page, mark the end with -30- or ###.

rubrics_metrics.name: Email Release Formatting and Summary
rubrics_metrics.description: For email-only releases, formatting can be more flexible; most reporters and editors favor text-only email releases, preferring a 200-300 word summary hyperlinked to the full release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the main text in the message window rather than as attachments. Provide a short summary (200–300 words) with a hyperlink to the full release and to images; make it easy for editors to decide quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia Handling (attachments vs. links)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of digital technology, online/electronic releases can contain photos, audio and video, although the media much prefer hyperlinks to these items than attachments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link rather than attach media; attachments may contain viruses and are often difficult to work with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedding popular search terms throughout the text to get search-engine pickup is a technique that can be fraught — it may look forced, unnatural or manipulative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While SEO can increase visibility, don't sacrifice natural readable language; overly optimized language may cause recipients to ignore or block future releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up Etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow-up after distribution by calling, emailing or meeting recipients to see if they need more information or assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not badger reporters and editors or call to confirm they received the release; be considerate and helpful — courteous follow-up is remembered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miscellaneous / Optional Production Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Add production code (at bottom left or right side of last page); single space the last paragraph or sentence on the final page if it will eliminate a sheet of paper; include a brief boilerplate description of your organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sample production-code format (month, day, year plus number of pages and subject). Include boilerplate with contact/website info as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate Description
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a brief boilerplate description of your organization (short paragraph about the organization, contact phone or website).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concise background that reporters can reuse; place near the end of the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness / Suitable Topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventional topics for releases: new products/services/patents; product and service sales; financial and investor information; fundraising results; business plans; survey results/research studies; new plants/stores/offices/hires; social responsibility activities; positions on legislation/issues/crises; trends and issues; inventions/discoveries; new lines of business; laws and regulations; new construction; special events; public alerts; VIP visits; official announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this list to evaluate whether an item merits a release — releases should convey newsworthy information about the company or organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution Beyond Media (audience targeting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many practitioners disseminate releases beyond the media to key audiences such as employees and investors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, send releases to stakeholders who care about the information, not just the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: End Markers and Continuation Notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Number the pages; put 'more' or 'continued' at the bottom of each page. Put -30- or ### to mark the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these conventions so editors know the release continues or has ended; useful for print and fax workflows.
